review_rows.answer: Purpose: support evidence-based participation, retention, and completion activities for high-need postsecondary students.
High-need students include low-income, first-generation, caregiver, disabled, dropout, reentering justice-impacted, and military-connected students. No numeric income cutoff is supplied here.

Eligible entities are public higher-education institutions, nonprofit educational organization/institution partnerships, or institution consortia. Eligible Indian entities govern, operate, or control Tribal Colleges or Universities. A nonprofit alone is not one of the ordinary eligible-entity categories.

Education Secretary competitively awards student-service grants for FY2027–2032. Applicants must supply attainment/completion or graduation plans; evidence tier and high-need focus; annual outcome benchmarks and evaluation plan; Pell receipt rates and demographics; reform-use description and post-grant sustainability. Application timing/manner are set by the Secretary.

Application reform choices cover comprehensive academic/career/student services, accelerated learning including dual enrollment/early college, scheduling or credit policy reforms, and transfer pathways. At least one such reform/practice must be described.

Grant spending must implement submitted plans and evidence-based participation/retention/completion reforms. Illustrative uses cover student services, academic and emergency financial support, career preparation and workforce experiences, and faculty/instructional-staff recruitment and retention. These examples are not a universal cash benefit.

Secretary must fund evaluations by grants/contracts and dissemination; evaluation checks implementation and compares participant completion/retention with similar-background nonparticipants. Final congressional report is due within 18 months after enactment.
An eligible entity with a branch campus may receive a grant for only one campus at a time.

Completion rate means two-year institution graduation OR transfer to a four-year institution, but four-year institution graduation. Tier 1 is promising prior research; tier 2 measures impact/cost effectiveness and rigorous successful implementation; tier 3 adds sizable important impacts and the text's reproduction/sustainability and effectiveness-condition language.

Mandatory reservation: 2% | Of the total amount appropriated for the Act in a fiscal year, reserved for eligible Indian entity grants to improve high-need student participation, retention, completion. Not 2% of an already reduced balance.
Program authorization; no fixed dollar amount | Competitive eligible-entity student-service grants for each FY2027–2032. This authorizes awards; it does not itself specify an appropriation amount.

Mandatory minimum reservation: at least 20% | Of fiscal-year appropriations NOT reserved by §4, for eligible-entity applications with at least one tier-3 reform/practice and the rest tier 1 or 2. Not 20% of original gross appropriations.
Discretionary maximum set-aside: 5% | Administration, capacity building, research, evaluation, reporting; denominator is fiscal-year funds NOT reserved under §4 OR §5(d).
Discretionary maximum set-aside: 2% | Technical assistance to eligible entities AND eligible Indian entities; same residual denominator as M04. Not the mandatory tribal reservation M01.

Required use restriction; no dollar amount | Recipient grant funds must carry out submitted plans and evidence-based reforms. Possible spending includes faculty/peer counseling, real-time progress data, transfer success, re-enrollment/staying-on-track incentives; tutoring/academic support/enrichment combined with emergency financial assistance; career coaching/planning, lower student/advisor ratios, networks/work-based learning, pathways and high-skill/high-wage/in-demand experience; recruiting/retaining faculty/instructional staff. No benefit size or individual entitlement stated.

Express emergency assistance and incentives; no dollar amount | Emergency financial assistance is listed with tutoring/academic/enrichment supports; re-enrollment or staying-on-track incentives are listed among student services. Neither is an independent appropriation.

Required evaluation grants/contracts; no fixed dollar amount | Secretary shall make grants or contracts with one or more organizations to evaluate reforms and disseminate impact information; evaluation requirements and 18-month final report apply. Do not double-count as an additional specified appropriation.
Application financial information; not new aid | Applicants report rates of Pell Grant receipt. This does not change Pell Grant amounts or eligibility.

output_items.display_text:
Source text (not simplified): Required Uses of Funds.--An eligible entity or eligible Indian 
entity that receives a grant under this Act shall use the grant funds 
to carry out the plans submitted under subsection (c) and for evidence-
based reforms and practices for improving participation, retention, and 
completion rates of students that may include the following:
            (1) Student services to support retention, completion, and 
        success, which may include--
                    (A) faculty and peer counseling;
                    (B) use of real-time data on student progress;
                    (C) improving transfer student success; and
                    (D) incentives for students to re-enroll or stay on 
                track.
            (2) Direct student support services, including a 
        combination of--
                    (A) tutoring, academic supports, and enrichment 
                services; and
                    (B) emergency financial assistance.
            (3) Efforts to prepare students for a career, which may 
        include--
                    (A) career coaching, career counseling and planning 
                services, and efforts to lower student to advisor 
                ratios;
                    (B) networking and work-based learning 
                opportunities to support the development of skills and 
                professional relationships;
                    (C) utilizing career pathways; and
                    (D) boosting experiences necessary to obtain and 
                succeed in high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand industry 
                sectors or occupations, as described in section 
                135(b)(3) of the Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical 
                Education Act of 2006 (20 U.S.C. 2355(b)(3)).
            (4) Efforts to recruit and retain faculty and other 
        instructional staff.

line_items.display_text:
Source text (not simplified): Required Uses of Funds.--An eligible entity or eligible Indian 
entity that receives a grant under this Act shall use the grant funds 
to carry out the plans submitted under subsection (c) and for evidence-
based reforms and practices for improving participation, retention, and 
completion rates of students that may include the following:
            (1) Student services to support retention, completion, and 
        success, which may include--
                    (A) faculty and peer counseling;
                    (B) use of real-time data on student progress;
                    (C) improving transfer student success; and
                    (D) incentives for students to re-enroll or stay on 
                track.
            (2) Direct student support services, including a 
        combination of--
                    (A) tutoring, academic supports, and enrichment 
                services; and
                    (B) emergency financial assistance.
            (3) Efforts to prepare students for a career, which may 
        include--
                    (A) career coaching, career counseling and planning 
                services, and efforts to lower student to advisor 
                ratios;
                    (B) networking and work-based learning 
                opportunities to support the development of skills and 
                professional relationships;
                    (C) utilizing career pathways; and
                    (D) boosting experiences necessary to obtain and 
                succeed in high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand industry 
                sectors or occupations, as described in section 
                135(b)(3) of the Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical 
                Education Act of 2006 (20 U.S.C. 2355(b)(3)).
            (4) Efforts to recruit and retain faculty and other 
        instructional staff.

Required Uses of Funds.--An eligible entity or eligible Indian 
entity that receives a grant under this Act shall use the grant funds 
to carry out the plans submitted under subsection (c) and for evidence-
based reforms and practices for improving participation, retention, and 
completion rates of students that may include the following:
            (1) Student services to support retention, completion, and 
        success, which may include--
                    (A) faculty and peer counseling;
                    (B) use of real-time data on student progress;
                    (C) improving transfer student success; and
                    (D) incentives for students to re-enroll or stay on 
                track.
            (2) Direct student support services, including a 
        combination of--
                    (A) tutoring, academic supports, and enrichment 
                services; and
                    (B) emergency financial assistance.
            (3) Efforts to prepare students for a career, which may 
        include--
                    (A) career coaching, career counseling and planning 
                services, and efforts to lower student to advisor 
                ratios;
                    (B) networking and work-based learning 
                opportunities to support the development of skills and 
                professional relationships;
                    (C) utilizing career pathways; and
                    (D) boosting experiences necessary to obtain and 
                succeed in high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand industry 
                sectors or occupations, as described in section 
                135(b)(3) of the Carl D. Perkins Career and Technical 
                Education Act of 2006 (20 U.S.C. 2355(b)(3)).
            (4) Efforts to recruit and retain faculty and other 
        instructional staff.

review_rows.answer: Purpose: support evidence-based participation, retention, and completion activities for high-need postsecondary students.
High-need students include low-income, first-generation, caregiver, disabled, dropout, reentering justice-impacted, and military-connected students. No numeric income cutoff is supplied here.

Eligible entities are public higher-education institutions, nonprofit educational organization/institution partnerships, or institution consortia. Eligible Indian entities govern, operate, or control Tribal Colleges or Universities. A nonprofit alone is not one of the ordinary eligible-entity categories.

Education Secretary competitively awards student-service grants for FY2027–2032. Applicants must supply attainment/completion or graduation plans; evidence tier and high-need focus; annual outcome benchmarks and evaluation plan; Pell receipt rates and demographics; reform-use description and post-grant sustainability. Application timing/manner are set by the Secretary.

Application reform choices cover comprehensive academic/career/student services, accelerated learning including dual enrollment/early college, scheduling or credit policy reforms, and transfer pathways. At least one such reform/practice must be described.

Grant spending must implement submitted plans and evidence-based participation/retention/completion reforms. Illustrative uses cover student services, academic and emergency financial support, career preparation and workforce experiences, and faculty/instructional-staff recruitment and retention. These examples are not a universal cash benefit.

Secretary must fund evaluations by grants/contracts and dissemination; evaluation checks implementation and compares participant completion/retention with similar-background nonparticipants. Final congressional report is due within 18 months after enactment.
An eligible entity with a branch campus may receive a grant for only one campus at a time.

Completion rate means two-year institution graduation OR transfer to a four-year institution, but four-year institution graduation. Tier 1 is promising prior research; tier 2 measures impact/cost effectiveness and rigorous successful implementation; tier 3 adds sizable important impacts and the text's reproduction/sustainability and effectiveness-condition language.

Mandatory reservation: 2% | Of the total amount appropriated for the Act in a fiscal year, reserved for eligible Indian entity grants to improve high-need student participation, retention, completion. Not 2% of an already reduced balance.
Program authorization; no fixed dollar amount | Competitive eligible-entity student-service grants for each FY2027–2032. This authorizes awards; it does not itself specify an appropriation amount.

Mandatory minimum reservation: at least 20% | Of fiscal-year appropriations NOT reserved by §4, for eligible-entity applications with at least one tier-3 reform/practice and the rest tier 1 or 2. Not 20% of original gross appropriations.
Discretionary maximum set-aside: 5% | Administration, capacity building, research, evaluation, reporting; denominator is fiscal-year funds NOT reserved under §4 OR §5(d).
Discretionary maximum set-aside: 2% | Technical assistance to eligible entities AND eligible Indian entities; same residual denominator as M04. Not the mandatory tribal reservation M01.

Required use restriction; no dollar amount | Recipient grant funds must carry out submitted plans and evidence-based reforms. Possible spending includes faculty/peer counseling, real-time progress data, transfer success, re-enrollment/staying-on-track incentives; tutoring/academic support/enrichment combined with emergency financial assistance; career coaching/planning, lower student/advisor ratios, networks/work-based learning, pathways and high-skill/high-wage/in-demand experience; recruiting/retaining faculty/instructional staff. No benefit size or individual entitlement stated.

Express emergency assistance and incentives; no dollar amount | Emergency financial assistance is listed with tutoring/academic/enrichment supports; re-enrollment or staying-on-track incentives are listed among student services. Neither is an independent appropriation.

Required evaluation grants/contracts; no fixed dollar amount | Secretary shall make grants or contracts with one or more organizations to evaluate reforms and disseminate impact information; evaluation requirements and 18-month final report apply. Do not double-count as an additional specified appropriation.
Application financial information; not new aid | Applicants report rates of Pell Grant receipt. This does not change Pell Grant amounts or eligibility.

review_rows.answer: Creates adjustment routes for qualifying childhood arrivals (Dream Act title I) and qualifying TPS/DED populations (American Promise Act title II), with shared application/protection rules. It is not an automatic citizenship grant.

Title I covers inadmissible/deportable persons, DED grantees, TPS holders, and sons/daughters of listed E(i), E(ii), H(i)(b), or L nonimmigrants, subject to all criteria: physical presence since Jan. 1, 2021; entry at 18 or younger and continuous residence since entry; specified admissibility, persecution and criminal/security restrictions; and one educational route. DACA is not required.

Educational routes: admission to higher education or postsecondary career/technical school; listed US high-school/equivalent/secondary career credential or recognized postsecondary credential; or enrollment in secondary school or programs leading to the listed diplomas, tests or credentials. Persons 18 or younger satisfying the other criteria receive reasonable opportunity to meet education requirements and may not face commenced/continued removal proceedings.

Title I bars include cited INA criminal/security grounds, any felony, three qualifying separate-date/separate-act misdemeanors, and domestic-violence misdemeanors (victim-related exception). State immigration-status offenses and minor traffic offenses are excluded; specified cannabis and nonviolent civil-disobedience exceptions apply to the misdemeanor count. Humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest waivers cover listed inadmissibility grounds and certain misdemeanors: one after 5 conviction-free years, up to two after 10. Felony means punishable by more than 1 year; misdemeanor more than 5 days through 1 year.

Even otherwise eligible title-I applicants face nondelegable provisional-denial discretion based on clear and convincing evidence including credible law-enforcement information: qualifying misdemeanor punishable by more than 30 days or secure-facility juvenile disposition PLUS significant continuing public-safety threat; or knowing/willful/voluntary participation in gang offenses with furtherance intent in the preceding 5 years. Listed minor/cannabis/nonviolent civil-disobedience/status-offense exclusions, mitigation/recency factors, and prohibition on database gang allegations establishing participation apply.

Provisional-denial protections: specific notice/evidence, at least 90 days to respond, second notice within 30 days, reopening for good cause including nonreceipt, 60 days to seek district-court review; de novo review on administrative record with applicant supplementation and agency rebuttal, then remand. Counsel required and appointed upon request; procedures due within 90 days after enactment.

Conditional residence lasts 10 years unless extended. Revocation only for ceasing to meet §102(b)(1)(C), after notice and hearing opportunity. Expiration/revocation returns the person to prior immigration status.

Removing conditions requires continued §102(b)(1)(C) eligibility and no abandonment, plus degree OR 2 good-standing years toward specified degree/credential; OR 2 years Uniformed Service with honorable discharge if discharged; OR earned-income duration described in M05. Hardship exception requires those first two conditions, compelling inability to meet the activity requirement, and disability, full-time caregiving, or specified hardship to self or qualifying spouse/parent/child. Referenced INA §312(a) requirements also apply unless disability prevents meeting them.

Conditions may be removed whenever eligible. Already-qualified initial applicants receive residence without conditions, with hardship/disability exceptions, one identical background check rather than duplication, and substituted fee (M04). Conditional time counts as lawful permanent residence for the referenced naturalization provisions, but naturalization applications are barred while conditional.

Repeals IIRIRA §505 / 8 USC 1623 concerning higher-education residency benefits, effective as if included in the original 1996 enactment. The precise preexisting restriction/economic effect is external context, not supplied by this bill.

Title II: apply within 3 years after enactment; at least 3 years continuous physical presence; specified admissibility rules. TPS route requires nationality/last habitual residence in a state designated Jan. 1, 2017 and TPS or otherwise eligibility then despite listed provisions, plus no subsequent disqualifying conduct. DED route requires eligibility Jan. 20, 2021 and no subsequent disqualifying conduct. Waivers for listed grounds are humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest and exclude convictions disqualifying under cited TPS law.

Title II inserts “as having been inspected and admitted into the United States, and” into INA §244(f)(4). Do not infer unlimited admission rights from this fragment or silently resolve the surrounding statute.

Shared rules: biometrics/biographics with physical-impairment alternative; completed satisfactory security/law-enforcement checks before adjustment; expunged/set-aside/rehabilitative judgments excluded from specified conviction meanings. Title I also requires Selective Service registration when applicable.

Prima-facie eligible people get reasonable application opportunity and protection from removal until final ineligibility, subject to the criminal/security judicial-review exception. Existing removal/voluntary-departure orders do not bar application or require a separate reopening motion; approval cancels removal, denial restores enforceability only after remedies exhausted. Applicants may seek advance parole while pending, and listed protected/pending individuals get work authorization upon application. Withdrawal closes processing without prejudicing future benefits applications.

Notice to appear does not stop presence/residence. Normally physical presence fails after a single absence exceeding 90 days or aggregate exceeding 180; residence fails after an absence exceeding 180 days unless nonabandonment shown. Extensions for beyond-control circumstances include illness, specified relatives' death/illness, document delays, COVID travel restrictions. Authorized travel is not counted.

Secretary may waive physical presence for people removed/departed on/after Jan. 20, 2017 with at least 4 years prior continuous physical presence, for humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest reasons; must establish overseas procedure with State for those otherwise eligible but for departure/removal. No numerical cap on residence grants.

Administrative appellate process due 30 days after enactment; district-court review available. Generally no removal during review until final ineligibility; criminal/security removal while judicial review pending is allowed without extinguishing review, with prompt return after reversal.

Documentary routes cover identity, entry/presence/nonabandonment, college admission/degree, secondary credentials/enrollment, fees, hardship, service and earned income. Many allow credible alternative evidence. Fee/hardship affidavits have specified unrelated-affiant and knowledge/contact/relationship requirements. Secretary can restrict unreliable/fraud-prone document classes only after Federal Register publication and public-comment opportunity.

Interim final implementation rules due 90 days after enactment, effective on publication, allowing immediate applications; finalize within 180 days of publication. Paperwork Reduction Act does not apply to implementation.

Application/DACA information generally cannot be used/disclosed for immigration enforcement; sole-information enforcement referrals prohibited. Bill adjustment-application information may be shared for application assistance, fraud, national security, or investigation/prosecution of non-immigration-status felonies. Knowing misuse penalty is M09.

Competitive USCIS nonprofit grants support outreach, authorized-practice application assistance, citizenship/civics/English/GED instruction and adjustment/citizenship assistance. Eligibility here does not bar another legally available status. Annual provisional-denial outcome reports begin within 1 year after enactment.
Optional application fee, cost-commensurate, capped at $495.00 | Title-I application processing; §303(c) exemption applies. This is a fee ceiling, not spending or a universal mandatory charge.

DACA streamlined route: no application fee, with exception | Granted DACA and renewal eligibility under Jan. 1, 2017 program terms required. Procedure has no fee, except cost-commensurate fee may be charged to those initially qualifying for nonconditional residence, subject to §303(c). No separate numeric cap supplied for that exception.
Optional cost-commensurate reasonable processing fee; no fixed dollar cap | Removing conditions; §303(c) exemptions. No dollar amount is supplied.
Fee substitution, not double charging | Initially eligible nonconditional applicants pay fee required under §104(a)(4), subject to §303(c), but do NOT pay §102(b)(3) application fee.

Earned-income eligibility duration / percentage, not tax or benefit amount | Earned income for periods totaling at least 3 years AND at least 75% of time with valid work authorization is one alternative to education/service for removing conditions. Listed enrollment periods reduce the total 3-year requirement. No minimum dollar income is stated.

Higher-education benefit rule repeal; no dollar amount | Repeals IIRIRA §505 / 8 USC 1623, retroactive to original enactment; does not itself specify tuition aid or spending. Preexisting provision's detailed effect unresolved.
Required reasonable cost-commensurate application fee, maximum $1,140 | Title-II adjustment processing; subject to §303(c) exemption; title-II applications due within 3 years after enactment.

Discretionary application-fee exemption / income threshold | Applicant may be exempt if 18 or younger OR prior 12-month total income less than 150% of Federal poverty line OR foster care/no parental or familial support OR inability to care for self due to serious chronic disability. These are alternatives, not cumulative criteria. Threshold is not a grant amount. FPL definition incorporates INA §213A(h); dollar threshold unresolved. Evidence includes age/identity, government earnings records/bank records or two unrelated knowledgeable affidavits, and two such affidavits for support/disability circumstances with specified contents.

Fine, maximum $10,000 | Any person knowingly using/publishing/permitting examination of information contrary to §309; not an immigration application fee or appropriation. No fixed collection total/time window stated.

Competitive grant program; restricted uses, no fixed dollar award | USCIS grants to eligible nonprofits for public information, screening/application/document help within authorized immigration practice, and rights/responsibilities, civics/English/GED and adjustment/citizenship assistance. No numeric grantee cap, match or individual entitlement specified.

Authorization of appropriations: “such sums as may be necessary” | Each FY2026–2036 for §310 program only; amounts appropriated remain available until expended. This is an unquantified authorization, not a fixed dollar appropriation and not zero spending.

Mandatory additional surcharge: $25 when a fee is charged | Funds appointed counsel for judicial review of provisional denials. Express exceptions: “as provided in section 302” and applicants fee-exempt under §303(c). Preserve §302 cross-reference; §302 itself states no fee schedule or clear financial exception. Do not silently correct it or invent a biometrics fee.

Earmarked receipts / account and indefinite availability; no aggregate dollar cap | Establishes Immigration Counsel Account in Treasury general fund; surcharge deposited and remains available until expended solely for appointed counsel required by Act. Every 2 years from account establishment, DHS reports balances and recommends fee changes aiming receipts for succeeding 2 years to approximate counsel costs. Recommendation is not automatic fee change.

Appointed-counsel funding direction; no separate dollar authorization | Judicial-review applicant must be represented; appointment upon request; AG procedures due 90 days after enactment; funded from §312 account receipts. Not a second $25 charge or separate fixed appropriation.

Earned-income documentation, not spending/tax obligation | Government-maintained records or, when unavailable, at least two reliable document types (bank/business/employer or contractor/worker-organization records, qualifying affidavits, remittances, or other credible evidence). Tax receipts, insurance, rent, mortgages, remittances and bank transactions also appear as presence documentation, not new taxes/fees/debt relief.

output_items.display_text:
Source text (not simplified): Grounds of ineligibility.--Except as provided in 
        paragraph (2), an alien is ineligible for adjustment of status 
        under this title (whether on a conditional basis or without the 
        conditional basis as provided in section 104(c)(2)) if any of 
        the following apply:
                    (A) The alien is inadmissible under paragraph (2) 
                or (3) of section 212(a) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1182(a)).
                    (B) Excluding any offense under State law for which 
                an essential element is the alien's immigration status, 
                and any minor traffic offense, the alien has been 
                convicted of--
                            (i) any felony offense;
                            (ii) three or more misdemeanor offenses 
                        (excluding simple possession of cannabis or 
                        cannabis-related paraphernalia, any offense 
                        involving cannabis or cannabis-related 
                        paraphernalia which is no longer prosecutable 
                        in the State in which the conviction was 
                        entered, and any offense involving civil 
                        disobedience without violence) not occurring on 
                        the same date, and not arising out of the same 
                        act, omission, or scheme of misconduct; or
                            (iii) a misdemeanor offense of domestic 
                        violence, unless the alien demonstrates that 
                        such crime is related to the alien having 
                        been--
                                    (I) a victim of domestic violence, 
                                sexual assault, stalking, child abuse 
                                or neglect, abuse or neglect in later 
                                life, or human trafficking;
                                    (II) battered or subjected to 
                                extreme cruelty; or
                                    (III) a victim of criminal activity 
                                described in section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii) 
                                of the Immigration and Nationality Act 
                                (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii)).

section_path.label: Sec. 102
section_path.heading: PERMANENT RESIDENT STATUS ON A CONDITIONAL BASIS FOR CERTAIN

line_items.display_text:
Source text (not simplified): Grounds of ineligibility.--Except as provided in 
        paragraph (2), an alien is ineligible for adjustment of status 
        under this title (whether on a conditional basis or without the 
        conditional basis as provided in section 104(c)(2)) if any of 
        the following apply:
                    (A) The alien is inadmissible under paragraph (2) 
                or (3) of section 212(a) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1182(a)).
                    (B) Excluding any offense under State law for which 
                an essential element is the alien's immigration status, 
                and any minor traffic offense, the alien has been 
                convicted of--
                            (i) any felony offense;
                            (ii) three or more misdemeanor offenses 
                        (excluding simple possession of cannabis or 
                        cannabis-related paraphernalia, any offense 
                        involving cannabis or cannabis-related 
                        paraphernalia which is no longer prosecutable 
                        in the State in which the conviction was 
                        entered, and any offense involving civil 
                        disobedience without violence) not occurring on 
                        the same date, and not arising out of the same 
                        act, omission, or scheme of misconduct; or
                            (iii) a misdemeanor offense of domestic 
                        violence, unless the alien demonstrates that 
                        such crime is related to the alien having 
                        been--
                                    (I) a victim of domestic violence, 
                                sexual assault, stalking, child abuse 
                                or neglect, abuse or neglect in later 
                                life, or human trafficking;
                                    (II) battered or subjected to 
                                extreme cruelty; or
                                    (III) a victim of criminal activity 
                                described in section 101(a)(15)(U)(iii) 
                                of the Immigration and Nationality Act 
                                (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(15)(U)(iii)).

In general.--Subject to paragraph (2), the Secretary 
        shall remove the conditional basis of an alien's permanent 
        resident status granted under this title and grant the alien 
        status as an alien lawfully admitted for permanent residence if 
        the alien--

(i) has obtained a degree from an institution of 
                higher education, or has completed at least 2 years, in 
                good standing, of a program in the United States 
                leading to a bachelor's degree or higher degree or a 
                recognized postsecondary credential from an area career 
                and technical education school providing education at 
                the postsecondary level;

(ii) has served in the Uniformed Services for at 
                least 2 years and, if discharged, received an honorable 
                discharge; or
                    (iii) demonstrates earned income for periods 
                totaling at least 3 years and at least 75 percent of 
                the time that the alien has had a valid employment 
                authorization, except that, in the case of an alien who 
                was enrolled in an institution of higher education, an 
                area career and technical education school to obtain a 
                recognized postsecondary credential, or an education 
                program described in section 102(b)(1)(D)(iii), the 
                Secretary shall reduce such total 3-year requirement by 
                the total of such periods of enrollment.

review_rows.answer: Creates adjustment routes for qualifying childhood arrivals (Dream Act title I) and qualifying TPS/DED populations (American Promise Act title II), with shared application/protection rules. It is not an automatic citizenship grant.

Title I covers inadmissible/deportable persons, DED grantees, TPS holders, and sons/daughters of listed E(i), E(ii), H(i)(b), or L nonimmigrants, subject to all criteria: physical presence since Jan. 1, 2021; entry at 18 or younger and continuous residence since entry; specified admissibility, persecution and criminal/security restrictions; and one educational route. DACA is not required.

Educational routes: admission to higher education or postsecondary career/technical school; listed US high-school/equivalent/secondary career credential or recognized postsecondary credential; or enrollment in secondary school or programs leading to the listed diplomas, tests or credentials. Persons 18 or younger satisfying the other criteria receive reasonable opportunity to meet education requirements and may not face commenced/continued removal proceedings.

Title I bars include cited INA criminal/security grounds, any felony, three qualifying separate-date/separate-act misdemeanors, and domestic-violence misdemeanors (victim-related exception). State immigration-status offenses and minor traffic offenses are excluded; specified cannabis and nonviolent civil-disobedience exceptions apply to the misdemeanor count. Humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest waivers cover listed inadmissibility grounds and certain misdemeanors: one after 5 conviction-free years, up to two after 10. Felony means punishable by more than 1 year; misdemeanor more than 5 days through 1 year.

Even otherwise eligible title-I applicants face nondelegable provisional-denial discretion based on clear and convincing evidence including credible law-enforcement information: qualifying misdemeanor punishable by more than 30 days or secure-facility juvenile disposition PLUS significant continuing public-safety threat; or knowing/willful/voluntary participation in gang offenses with furtherance intent in the preceding 5 years. Listed minor/cannabis/nonviolent civil-disobedience/status-offense exclusions, mitigation/recency factors, and prohibition on database gang allegations establishing participation apply.

Provisional-denial protections: specific notice/evidence, at least 90 days to respond, second notice within 30 days, reopening for good cause including nonreceipt, 60 days to seek district-court review; de novo review on administrative record with applicant supplementation and agency rebuttal, then remand. Counsel required and appointed upon request; procedures due within 90 days after enactment.

Conditional residence lasts 10 years unless extended. Revocation only for ceasing to meet §102(b)(1)(C), after notice and hearing opportunity. Expiration/revocation returns the person to prior immigration status.

Removing conditions requires continued §102(b)(1)(C) eligibility and no abandonment, plus degree OR 2 good-standing years toward specified degree/credential; OR 2 years Uniformed Service with honorable discharge if discharged; OR earned-income duration described in M05. Hardship exception requires those first two conditions, compelling inability to meet the activity requirement, and disability, full-time caregiving, or specified hardship to self or qualifying spouse/parent/child. Referenced INA §312(a) requirements also apply unless disability prevents meeting them.

Conditions may be removed whenever eligible. Already-qualified initial applicants receive residence without conditions, with hardship/disability exceptions, one identical background check rather than duplication, and substituted fee (M04). Conditional time counts as lawful permanent residence for the referenced naturalization provisions, but naturalization applications are barred while conditional.

Repeals IIRIRA §505 / 8 USC 1623 concerning higher-education residency benefits, effective as if included in the original 1996 enactment. The precise preexisting restriction/economic effect is external context, not supplied by this bill.

Title II: apply within 3 years after enactment; at least 3 years continuous physical presence; specified admissibility rules. TPS route requires nationality/last habitual residence in a state designated Jan. 1, 2017 and TPS or otherwise eligibility then despite listed provisions, plus no subsequent disqualifying conduct. DED route requires eligibility Jan. 20, 2021 and no subsequent disqualifying conduct. Waivers for listed grounds are humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest and exclude convictions disqualifying under cited TPS law.

Title II inserts “as having been inspected and admitted into the United States, and” into INA §244(f)(4). Do not infer unlimited admission rights from this fragment or silently resolve the surrounding statute.

Shared rules: biometrics/biographics with physical-impairment alternative; completed satisfactory security/law-enforcement checks before adjustment; expunged/set-aside/rehabilitative judgments excluded from specified conviction meanings. Title I also requires Selective Service registration when applicable.

Prima-facie eligible people get reasonable application opportunity and protection from removal until final ineligibility, subject to the criminal/security judicial-review exception. Existing removal/voluntary-departure orders do not bar application or require a separate reopening motion; approval cancels removal, denial restores enforceability only after remedies exhausted. Applicants may seek advance parole while pending, and listed protected/pending individuals get work authorization upon application. Withdrawal closes processing without prejudicing future benefits applications.

Notice to appear does not stop presence/residence. Normally physical presence fails after a single absence exceeding 90 days or aggregate exceeding 180; residence fails after an absence exceeding 180 days unless nonabandonment shown. Extensions for beyond-control circumstances include illness, specified relatives' death/illness, document delays, COVID travel restrictions. Authorized travel is not counted.

Secretary may waive physical presence for people removed/departed on/after Jan. 20, 2017 with at least 4 years prior continuous physical presence, for humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest reasons; must establish overseas procedure with State for those otherwise eligible but for departure/removal. No numerical cap on residence grants.

Administrative appellate process due 30 days after enactment; district-court review available. Generally no removal during review until final ineligibility; criminal/security removal while judicial review pending is allowed without extinguishing review, with prompt return after reversal.

Documentary routes cover identity, entry/presence/nonabandonment, college admission/degree, secondary credentials/enrollment, fees, hardship, service and earned income. Many allow credible alternative evidence. Fee/hardship affidavits have specified unrelated-affiant and knowledge/contact/relationship requirements. Secretary can restrict unreliable/fraud-prone document classes only after Federal Register publication and public-comment opportunity.

Interim final implementation rules due 90 days after enactment, effective on publication, allowing immediate applications; finalize within 180 days of publication. Paperwork Reduction Act does not apply to implementation.

Application/DACA information generally cannot be used/disclosed for immigration enforcement; sole-information enforcement referrals prohibited. Bill adjustment-application information may be shared for application assistance, fraud, national security, or investigation/prosecution of non-immigration-status felonies. Knowing misuse penalty is M09.

Competitive USCIS nonprofit grants support outreach, authorized-practice application assistance, citizenship/civics/English/GED instruction and adjustment/citizenship assistance. Eligibility here does not bar another legally available status. Annual provisional-denial outcome reports begin within 1 year after enactment.
Optional application fee, cost-commensurate, capped at $495.00 | Title-I application processing; §303(c) exemption applies. This is a fee ceiling, not spending or a universal mandatory charge.

DACA streamlined route: no application fee, with exception | Granted DACA and renewal eligibility under Jan. 1, 2017 program terms required. Procedure has no fee, except cost-commensurate fee may be charged to those initially qualifying for nonconditional residence, subject to §303(c). No separate numeric cap supplied for that exception.
Optional cost-commensurate reasonable processing fee; no fixed dollar cap | Removing conditions; §303(c) exemptions. No dollar amount is supplied.
Fee substitution, not double charging | Initially eligible nonconditional applicants pay fee required under §104(a)(4), subject to §303(c), but do NOT pay §102(b)(3) application fee.

Earned-income eligibility duration / percentage, not tax or benefit amount | Earned income for periods totaling at least 3 years AND at least 75% of time with valid work authorization is one alternative to education/service for removing conditions. Listed enrollment periods reduce the total 3-year requirement. No minimum dollar income is stated.

Higher-education benefit rule repeal; no dollar amount | Repeals IIRIRA §505 / 8 USC 1623, retroactive to original enactment; does not itself specify tuition aid or spending. Preexisting provision's detailed effect unresolved.
Required reasonable cost-commensurate application fee, maximum $1,140 | Title-II adjustment processing; subject to §303(c) exemption; title-II applications due within 3 years after enactment.

Discretionary application-fee exemption / income threshold | Applicant may be exempt if 18 or younger OR prior 12-month total income less than 150% of Federal poverty line OR foster care/no parental or familial support OR inability to care for self due to serious chronic disability. These are alternatives, not cumulative criteria. Threshold is not a grant amount. FPL definition incorporates INA §213A(h); dollar threshold unresolved. Evidence includes age/identity, government earnings records/bank records or two unrelated knowledgeable affidavits, and two such affidavits for support/disability circumstances with specified contents.

Fine, maximum $10,000 | Any person knowingly using/publishing/permitting examination of information contrary to §309; not an immigration application fee or appropriation. No fixed collection total/time window stated.

Competitive grant program; restricted uses, no fixed dollar award | USCIS grants to eligible nonprofits for public information, screening/application/document help within authorized immigration practice, and rights/responsibilities, civics/English/GED and adjustment/citizenship assistance. No numeric grantee cap, match or individual entitlement specified.

Authorization of appropriations: “such sums as may be necessary” | Each FY2026–2036 for §310 program only; amounts appropriated remain available until expended. This is an unquantified authorization, not a fixed dollar appropriation and not zero spending.

Mandatory additional surcharge: $25 when a fee is charged | Funds appointed counsel for judicial review of provisional denials. Express exceptions: “as provided in section 302” and applicants fee-exempt under §303(c). Preserve §302 cross-reference; §302 itself states no fee schedule or clear financial exception. Do not silently correct it or invent a biometrics fee.

Earmarked receipts / account and indefinite availability; no aggregate dollar cap | Establishes Immigration Counsel Account in Treasury general fund; surcharge deposited and remains available until expended solely for appointed counsel required by Act. Every 2 years from account establishment, DHS reports balances and recommends fee changes aiming receipts for succeeding 2 years to approximate counsel costs. Recommendation is not automatic fee change.

Appointed-counsel funding direction; no separate dollar authorization | Judicial-review applicant must be represented; appointment upon request; AG procedures due 90 days after enactment; funded from §312 account receipts. Not a second $25 charge or separate fixed appropriation.

Earned-income documentation, not spending/tax obligation | Government-maintained records or, when unavailable, at least two reliable document types (bank/business/employer or contractor/worker-organization records, qualifying affidavits, remittances, or other credible evidence). Tax receipts, insurance, rent, mortgages, remittances and bank transactions also appear as presence documentation, not new taxes/fees/debt relief.

review_rows.answer: The Laken Riley Act adds a mandatory-custody category under INA 236(c) involving both specified inadmissibility provisions AND specified crime-related triggers. It is not a rule covering every immigrant arrested for any crime. The title's theft label is narrower than the actual list.
